items.title: 20.3 Comparison of Reactivity of Benzene with Alkanes and Alkenes

source_refs.note: Topic 20.3 with Quick Check 20.3, answered (PDF 64). The book's sketch draws the crossed-out addition arrow on cyclohexene, which does add bromine; the lesson gives the comparison as a table. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Alkanes are generally unreactive, because they are non-polar and have only sigma bonds, although they undergo free-radical substitution quite easily in UV light. Alkenes are very reactive: their pi electrons are available to electrophiles, and they readily undergo electrophilic addition.
Benzene has pi electrons too, and like alkenes it reacts with electrophiles, but with two key differences:

items: Benzene is very stable and so less reactive.
Unlike alkenes, it undergoes electrophilic substitution, not electrophilic addition.

blocks.caption: Bromine with benzene and with cyclohexene
rows: Br2 with a FeBr3 (or AlBr3) catalyst
an H is replaced by Br; the aromatic ring is kept
two Br atoms add across the double bond

blocks.text: Substitution keeps the aromatic ring because of the extensive delocalisation of its pi electrons. The reaction does pass through an intermediate in which the aromaticity is lost, but it is restored when the reaction is complete, so the overall stability of the ring is not affected. Addition would destroy the delocalisation for good, so it is not favoured.
Benzene is highly unsaturated, yet it does not readily undergo addition reactions. Explain.
